**What you already know:** In P.5 you studied Uganda — its people and their settlement. In P.6 you widen the picture to the whole of East Africa working together.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: explain what the East African Community is and what regional cooperation means
name the member countries of the East African Community
describe the formation, collapse and revival of the former East African Community
state the objectives and benefits of the East African Community
name the organs of the East African Community and their roles
state the challenges facing the East African Community and how they can be reduced
explain trade and the common market in the EAC

sections.title: 1. What is the East African Community?

blocks.x: **East African Community (EAC):** The East African Community (EAC) is a regional organisation formed by countries of East Africa to work together for the benefit of their people. EAC stands for East African Community.

**Regional cooperation:** Regional cooperation is when countries in the same region work together to achieve common goals. East African countries cooperate to promote peace, trade, development and good relations among their people.

sections.title: 2. Which countries are members of the EAC?

blocks.x: The original East African Community was formed by **Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania**. Rwanda and Burundi later joined the East African Community.

The members of the East African Community today are **eight** countries: Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Rwanda, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda. Somalia became a member of the East African Community in 2024, so Somalia is the newest member of the EAC.

sections.title: 3. How did the former EAC and common services work?

blocks.x: The former East African Community was formed in **1967** by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. They formed the Community to work together and provide common services and promote development in East Africa.

**East African Common Services Organisation:** The East African Common Services Organisation was an organisation through which Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania provided and managed common services before the formation of the former EAC.

**East African High Commission:** The East African High Commission was an organisation through which Uganda, Kenya and Tanganyika worked together to manage common services before the East African Common Services Organisation.

**Common services:** Common services are services that are provided and used by more than one country. Examples of common services that were provided through cooperation among East African countries are railways, harbours, postal services, telecommunications, airways and research services. They helped the East African countries to share services and resources and reduce the cost of providing some services separately.

sections.title: 4. What are the objectives and benefits of the EAC?

blocks.x: The objectives of the East African Community are:

items: Promoting economic cooperation.
Promoting trade among member countries.
Promoting peace and security.
Improving the welfare of the people.
Promoting social and cultural cooperation.
Encouraging development among member countries.
Strengthening cooperation among member states.

blocks.x: The EAC promotes trade by encouraging member countries to buy and sell goods and services from one another. The EAC encourages member countries to work together and solve problems peacefully. The EAC promotes development by encouraging member countries to work together in areas such as trade, transport, education, health and infrastructure.
The benefits of the East African Community are:

items: Promoting trade.
Promoting peace and security.
Creating a larger market for goods and services.
Promoting movement of people.
Promoting tourism.
Encouraging cooperation in education.
Encouraging cooperation in health.
Improving transport and communication.
Creating employment opportunities.
Promoting social and cultural relations.

blocks.x: The EAC provides traders with a larger market where they can sell their goods and buy goods from other member countries. The EAC promotes tourism by encouraging people to visit different countries in East Africa. The EAC promotes cooperation in education and allows learners to learn about the people, cultures and countries of East Africa. The EAC brings East African countries together so that they can work towards common goals.

sections.title: 5. Why did the former EAC collapse?

blocks.x: The former East African Community collapsed in **1977**. The collapse of the EAC means that the former member countries stopped working together under the organisation.
Some of the causes of the collapse of the former EAC were:

items: Political differences among member countries.
Economic differences among member countries.
Different national interests.
Disagreements over how resources and benefits should be shared.
Poor cooperation among the member countries.
Differences in economic policies.

blocks.x: Political differences made it difficult for the member countries to agree on important matters. The countries had different economic conditions and interests, which caused disagreements about how benefits should be shared.
The effects of the collapse of the former EAC were:

items: Common services were separated.
Trade among the three countries was affected.
Cooperation among the countries reduced.
Some regional organisations and services stopped operating together.
People experienced difficulties in using some common services.
The countries lost some of the benefits of working together.

blocks.x: The collapse was a problem because it reduced cooperation among Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania and made it harder for the countries to enjoy the benefits of working together.

The East African Community was revived in **2000**. Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania revived the East African Community. It was revived because the countries recognised the importance of working together for economic and social development.
Some reasons for the revival of the EAC are:

items: To promote trade.
To promote economic development.
To strengthen cooperation.
To promote peace and security.
To improve relations among East African countries.
To create a larger market.
To improve the welfare of the people.

blocks.x: Expansion of the EAC means increasing the number of countries that belong to the Community. Rwanda and Burundi joined in 2007, South Sudan joined in 2016, the Democratic Republic of the Congo joined in 2022, and Somalia joined in 2024.

The EAC has expanded because more countries want to benefit from regional cooperation, trade, peace and development. More member countries provide a larger market, more opportunities for trade and stronger regional cooperation.
There are **eight** member countries of the EAC.

items: Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo are landlocked EAC member countries.
Kenya, Tanzania and Somalia have coastlines on the Indian Ocean.

sections.title: 8. What are the organs of the EAC?

blocks.x: An organ of the EAC is a body responsible for carrying out particular duties of the Community. The organs of the East African Community are:

items: The Summit
The Council of Ministers
The East African Legislative Assembly
The East African Court of Justice
The Secretariat

blocks.x: **The Summit** is made up of the Heads of State of the EAC partner countries. The Summit gives overall direction and guidance to the EAC.
**The Council of Ministers** is made up of ministers from the partner countries who are responsible for EAC matters. It makes decisions and gives direction on matters concerning the EAC.
**The East African Legislative Assembly** is the legislative organ of the EAC. It makes laws for the EAC and performs other duties given to it by the EAC Treaty.
**The East African Court of Justice** is the judicial organ of the EAC. It helps to interpret and apply the EAC Treaty and promotes justice within the Community.
**The Secretariat** is the executive and administrative organ of the EAC. The EAC Secretariat is headed by the Secretary General.
Some challenges facing the East African Community are:

items: Political differences.
Conflicts among member countries.
Different national interests.
Differences in economic development.
Trade disagreements.
Poor infrastructure in some areas.
Insecurity in some parts of the region.
Differences in policies and laws.

blocks.x: The challenges facing the EAC can be reduced by:

items: Promoting dialogue among member countries.
Solving conflicts peacefully.
Improving transport and communication.
Promoting fair trade.
Following EAC agreements.
Strengthening cooperation among member countries.

sections.title: 10. How does the EAC promote trade?

blocks.x: **Trade** is the buying and selling of goods and services. The EAC promotes trade by encouraging member countries to trade with one another and by reducing barriers to trade.

**Common market:** A common market is an arrangement where member countries allow the freer movement of goods, services, people, labour and capital among them. A common market is important to EAC countries because it provides a larger market and makes it easier for people and businesses to trade and work across member countries.

sections.title: 11. What are the symbols of the EAC?

blocks.x: The symbols of the East African Community are:

items: The EAC flag
The EAC emblem
The EAC anthem
The EAC motto

blocks.x: The EAC flag is a symbol of unity and identity among the member countries. The EAC motto is **One People, One Destiny**. It means that the people of East Africa should work together as one people towards a common future. The EAC anthem promotes unity, cooperation and a sense of belonging among the people of East Africa.

The EAC promotes unity by encouraging people from different East African countries to work, trade, study and interact together. The EAC encourages people to appreciate and share the different cultures of East Africa. Cooperation helps the countries to solve common problems, promote development and improve the lives of their people.

sections.title: 12. Where are the EAC countries on the map?

blocks.x: A P.6 learner should be able to locate the EAC member countries on a map of East Africa. The EAC countries a learner should be able to locate are Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Somalia.
The EAC countries that border Uganda are:

items: Kenya
South Sudan
Democratic Republic of the Congo
Rwanda
Tanzania

topics.title: Major Resources of East Africa
topics.heading: TOPIC 2: MAJOR RESOURCES OF EAST AFRICA

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Six Curriculum, Set One, Social Studies Topic 2, 30 periods (`curriculum/P6-SET-ONE-2010.pdf`, topic outline page 312 and pages 326–331).*
**What you already know:** In P.5 you studied the resources of **Uganda**. In P.6 you study the resources of the **whole of East Africa** — the land, the minerals, the water and the fishing industry.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: name the major resources of East Africa and locate them
describe land as a resource: plants, animals, cultivation and tourism
name the minerals of East Africa, the types of mining and where minerals are found
describe the drainage of East Africa and the uses of water
describe fishing methods, preservation, importance, problems and solutions

blocks.x: Definitions
**Resource:** Anything found in the environment that people use to satisfy their needs.
**Natural resource:** A resource provided by nature — land, water, minerals, vegetation, animals and climate.
The major resources of East Africa are **land, minerals, water, vegetation, wildlife, climate and the people themselves**.
(a) Plants (vegetation)

head: Vegetation type
Where in East Africa
rows: Mabira and Budongo (Uganda), Kakamega (Kenya), Kivu shores
Most of the region — the largest area
Slopes of Kilimanjaro, Mt Kenya, Elgon and Rwenzori
The Indian Ocean coast of Kenya and Tanzania
The Sudd edge, Lake Kyoga area, Kilombero

blocks.x: **Uses:** timber, poles, firewood and charcoal · medicine · pasture · raw materials for paper and furniture · protection of soil and water catchments · homes for wild animals · tourist attractions.
(b) Animals — domestic and wild

**Domestic animals:** cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, poultry, donkeys. Breeds of cattle include the local **Ankole long-horned** and **Zebu**, and the exotic **Friesian, Jersey and Guernsey**. They give meat, milk, hides and skins, manure, transport and money.

**Wild animals:** elephants, lions, buffaloes, giraffes, zebras, antelopes, rhinos, gorillas and chimpanzees. They attract **tourists**, are used for research and education, and are part of our heritage.
(c) Cultivation — cash and food crops

head: Crop type
Examples and where they are grown
rows: Coffee (Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania), tea (Kericho in Kenya, Fort Portal in Uganda), cotton (eastern Uganda, Tanzania), sugar cane (Kakira, Kinyara, Mumias), sisal (Tanga in Tanzania), pyrethrum (Kenya highlands), tobacco (West Nile), cloves (**Zanzibar and Pemba**), cashew nuts (southern Tanzania), vanilla (Uganda)
Matooke, maize, millet, sorghum, cassava, sweet potatoes, beans, groundnuts, rice, wheat

blocks.x: **Factors favouring crop growing:** fertile soils · reliable rainfall · suitable climate · availability of land and labour · markets and transport.
(d) Tourism
**Tourism:** Travelling to visit places of interest for pleasure, study or rest.

head: Attraction
Examples
rows: **Serengeti, Ngorongoro** (Tanzania); **Maasai Mara, Tsavo, Amboseli** (Kenya); **Murchison Falls, Queen Elizabeth, Kidepo, Bwindi** (Uganda); **Akagera** (Rwanda); **Ruvubu** (Burundi)
Kilimanjaro, Mt Kenya, Rwenzori, Elgon, Virunga volcanoes
Lake Victoria, the source of the Nile at Jinja, Murchison Falls, the Indian Ocean beaches
Kasubi Tombs, Fort Jesus in Mombasa, Bagamoyo, traditional dances, the Kigali Genocide Memorial

blocks.x: **Importance of tourism:** foreign exchange · employment · government revenue · market for crafts and food · development of roads, hotels and airports · international friendship.

**Problems of tourism:** poaching · insecurity and political unrest · poor roads to some parks · high cost of travel · destruction of habitats · few skilled guides · animals raiding gardens near parks.
Definitions
**Mineral:** A useful substance obtained from the earth by mining.
**Mining:** The process of removing minerals from the earth.
Minerals of East Africa and where they are found

head: Country
Minerals
rows: Copper (**Kilembe**), cobalt, limestone (**Hima, Tororo**), gold (Karamoja, Busia), salt (**Katwe**), iron ore (Muko), phosphates (Sukulu), oil (**Albertine Graben**)
Soda ash (**Lake Magadi**), fluorspar (Kerio Valley), limestone (Athi River), titanium (Kwale), gemstones, salt
Diamonds (**Mwadui**), gold (**Geita**), **tanzanite** (Mererani), natural gas (Songo Songo), coal (Kiwira), tin, phosphates

blocks.x: Types of mining

head: Type
How it is done
rows: Simple tools — hoes, pangas, pans and baskets; panning gold in river sand; digging shallow pits by hand
Removing the soil above and scooping the mineral with machines, as at Mwadui and Hima
Digging deep shafts and tunnels, as at Kilembe
Boring deep holes for oil and natural gas
Scooping minerals from river or lake beds

blocks.x: Minerals as a source of income

They earn **foreign exchange** when exported · provide **employment** · give government **taxes and royalties** · provide **raw materials** for industries such as cement and steel · lead to the growth of **towns and roads** where mines are opened.
Problems of the mining industry

Shortage of **capital** and modern machinery · **low level of technology** and few skilled people · minerals in **remote areas** with poor roads · **accidents** and mine collapses · **pollution** and land degradation · minerals in **small scattered deposits** · unstable **world prices** · **smuggling** and illegal mining · displacement of people.
**Solutions:** attract investment, train people in mining skills, improve roads to mining areas, enforce safety and environmental laws, add value by processing minerals at home, and fight smuggling.
Definition
**Drainage:** The way water is held and carried in an area by lakes, rivers, swamps, seas and oceans.
Lakes of East Africa

head: Lake
Notes
rows: The largest in Africa; shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania
The deepest in Africa; Tanzania, D.R. Congo, Burundi, Zambia

blocks.x: Lakes are of different kinds: **rift valley** lakes (Tanganyika, Albert, Turkana), **depression** lakes (Victoria, Kyoga), **crater** lakes (Katwe, Nyamunuka) and **man-made** lakes (behind dams).
Rivers of East Africa

**River Nile** (from Lake Victoria at Jinja, flowing north) · **Kagera** (the longest feeder of Lake Victoria) · **Tana** and **Athi–Galana** (Kenya) · **Rufiji, Pangani, Ruvuma, Ruaha** (Tanzania) · **Katonga, Semliki, Aswa** (Uganda) · **Ruvubu and Ruzizi** (Burundi and Rwanda).
**Other water bodies:** the **Indian Ocean** on the eastern side, and swamps such as those of Lake Kyoga, the Kilombero valley and Rwanda's Rugezi.
Uses of water in East Africa

Drinking and domestic use · **irrigation** (Mubuku, Doho, Mwea in Kenya) · **hydro-electric power** (Nalubaale, Kiira, Bujagali, Isimba, Karuma, Owen Falls; Kidatu in Tanzania) · **fishing** · **water transport** on lakes, rivers and the ocean · **tourism and sport** · industry · watering animals.
**Problems:** pollution from factories and towns · water hyacinth · silting · drying up of lakes and wetlands · floods · water-borne diseases · water shortage in dry areas.
Definition
**Fishing:** The catching of fish and other water animals for food and for sale.
Fishing grounds
Lake Victoria (the biggest) · Lakes Kyoga, Albert, Edward and George · Lake Tanganyika · Lake Turkana · the **Indian Ocean** coast · fish ponds on farms.
Common fish: **Nile perch (mputa), tilapia (ngege), silver fish (mukene), tuna, catfish, lungfish, sardines (dagaa)**.
Fishing methods

head: Traditional
Modern
rows: Trawling with large nets pulled by boats
Gill nets and long lines from motor boats
Fish farming in ponds and cages
Use of echo sounders and refrigerated boats

blocks.x: Preservation of fish

head: Traditional
Modern
rows: Modern processing factories, as at Jinja and Kisumu

blocks.x: Importance of fishing to the people of East Africa

**Food** rich in protein · **employment** for fishermen, traders and factory workers · **income** for families · **foreign exchange** from exported Nile perch fillets · **raw materials** for fish-processing and animal-feed industries · government **revenue** through licences and taxes · growth of **landing sites and towns**.
Problems of the fishing industry

items: **Over-fishing** and use of **undersized nets**, which catch immature fish.
Use of **poison and explosives**, which kill all life in the water.
**Water hyacinth** blocking landing sites.
**Water pollution** from factories, towns and farms.
**Poor preservation and transport**, so fish goes bad.
**Lack of capital** for modern boats and equipment.
**Accidents and storms** on the lakes; many fishermen cannot swim.
**Insecurity** and theft of nets and engines.
**Diseases** such as bilharzia at landing sites.
**Low prices** paid to the fishermen by middlemen.

blocks.x: Solutions

Enforce laws on **net sizes and closed seasons** · ban poison and explosives · encourage **fish farming** in ponds and cages · remove water hyacinth · build **cold rooms** and improve roads to landing sites · give **loans and training** to fishermen · provide life jackets and weather warnings · form **fishermen's cooperatives** so they get fair prices · patrol the lakes.

Mining by sinking deep shafts underground

items: Copper is mined at **Kilembe** in Uganda; diamonds at **Mwadui** and gold at **Geita** in Tanzania; soda ash at **Lake Magadi** in Kenya.
**Tanzanite** is found only in Tanzania.
Cloves are the main cash crop of **Zanzibar and Pemba**; pyrethrum is grown in the **Kenya highlands**; sisal at **Tanga**.
**Lake Victoria** is the largest lake in Africa; **Lake Tanganyika** is the deepest.

topics.heading: TOPIC 3: TRANSPORT AND COMMUNICATION IN EAST AFRICA

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Six Curriculum, Set One, Social Studies Topic 3, 25 periods (`curriculum/P6-SET-ONE-2010.pdf`, topic outline page 313 and pages 332–336).*

**What you already know:** You know how people in your village send messages and move from place to place. In P.6 you study **communication and transport in the whole of East Africa** — how they were done long ago, how they are done today, and the good and bad side of each.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: define communication and transport
describe traditional means of communication and their challenges
describe modern means of communication, their challenges and solutions
describe traditional and modern means of transport in East Africa
give the advantages and disadvantages of the different forms of transport

blocks.x: Definition
**Communication:** The sending and receiving of messages, information or ideas from one person or place to another.
Traditional means of communication

head: Means
How it was used
rows: Different beats announced war, death, a meeting, a ceremony or danger
To call for help when there was danger, a thief or a fire

topics.title: The Road to Independence in East Africa
topics.heading: TOPIC 4: THE ROAD TO INDEPENDENCE IN EAST AFRICA

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Six Curriculum, Set One, Social Studies Topic 4, 40 periods (`curriculum/P6-SET-ONE-2010.pdf`, topic outline page 314 and pages 337–343).*

**What you already know:** In P.5 you learnt a little about foreigners in Uganda. In P.6 you follow the whole story for **East Africa**: the explorers, the colonialists, the struggle for independence country by country, what happened after independence, and how **democracy and elections** work today.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: describe the explorers — who they were, when they came, how they came and why
describe colonial settlement, administration and its impact on East Africans
describe the struggle for independence in Kenya, Tanganyika, Uganda, Burundi and Rwanda
describe post-independence East Africa and its challenges
explain democracy, citizenship, rights and responsibilities and the electoral process

blocks.x: The explorers
**Explorer:** A person who travels to an unknown place in order to find out about it.

head: Explorer
When
What he did
rows: The first Europeans to see Mt Kilimanjaro and Mt Kenya
Reached Lake Tanganyika; Speke reached Lake Victoria
Reached the **source of the Nile at Jinja**
Reached Lake Albert and Murchison Falls
Explored Central and East Africa and fought the slave trade
Found Livingstone at Ujiji; sailed round Lake Victoria and wrote the letter inviting missionaries to Buganda

blocks.x: How and why they came

They came **by sea** to the coast and then walked inland with porters, using caravan routes. They came to find the **source of the Nile**, to **map** the interior, to look for **raw materials and markets**, to **spread Christianity**, to help **stop the slave trade**, and for **adventure and fame**. Many were sent by geographical societies or by their governments.
Their achievements

They mapped the lakes, rivers and mountains · they told Europe about East Africa · their reports helped to **end the slave trade** · they opened routes that later became roads and towns · they invited missionaries, who started schools and hospitals.
Challenges they faced

Tropical **diseases** such as malaria and sleeping sickness · **hostile people** who attacked them · **wild animals** · **thick forests, swamps, rivers and mountains** · **language barriers** · shortage of food and clean water · **desertion** by porters · long distances on foot.
Colonialists, settlement and administration
After the **Berlin Conference of 1884–85**, East Africa was shared out:

head: Country
Colonial master
rows: Britain (a **Colony**, with white settlers in the "White Highlands")
**Germany** first, then Britain after the First World War (as a mandated territory)
**Germany** first, then **Belgium** after the First World War

blocks.x: **Methods of administration:** the British used **indirect rule** — governing through existing chiefs, as with the Buganda Agreement of 1900. The Germans and the Belgians used mostly **direct rule**, with their own officers and appointed chiefs, and the Belgians in Rwanda and Burundi ruled through the king while deepening the divisions between groups.
Impact of colonialists on the people of East Africa

head: Positive
Negative
rows: Roads, railways and towns were built
Africans **lost their independence** and their land
Christianity, Islam and formal education spread
New cash crops — coffee, tea, cotton, sisal
Africans were made to grow crops for the coloniser
Money economy, trade and industries began
Borders divided tribes; new **ethnic divisions** were created
Peace was enforced between warring groups
Exploitation of raw materials and cheap labour

sections.title: 2. THE STRUGGLE FOR INDEPENDENCE, COUNTRY BY COUNTRY

blocks.x: Kenya Colony

items: Kenya had many **white settlers**, who had taken the fertile **White Highlands**, so the struggle was hard.
Early movements: the **Young Kikuyu Association** (Harry Thuku), the **Kikuyu Central Association**, and later **KAU** and **KANU**.
The **Mau Mau uprising (1952–1960)** was an armed struggle for land and freedom; a state of emergency was declared and **Jomo Kenyatta** was imprisoned.
Kenya became independent on **12 December 1963**, with **Jomo Kenyatta** as leader, and a republic in 1964.

blocks.x: Tanganyika (Tanzania) Territory

items: Africans resisted the Germans in the **Maji Maji rebellion (1905–1907)**.
**TANU** (Tanganyika African National Union) was formed in 1954 under **Julius Nyerere**.
The struggle was mainly **peaceful**, using meetings, newspapers and elections.
Tanganyika became independent on **9 December 1961** and a republic in 1962.
Zanzibar became independent in 1963 and had a revolution in January 1964; on **26 April 1964** Tanganyika and Zanzibar united to form **Tanzania**.

blocks.x: Uganda Protectorate

items: Political parties were formed: the **Uganda National Congress (1952)**, the **Democratic Party (DP)**, the **Uganda People's Congress (UPC)** and **Kabaka Yekka (KY)**.
Farmers' cooperatives, trade unions and the press pressed for self-rule.
Uganda became independent on **9 October 1962**, with **Milton Obote** as Prime Minister and the **Kabaka, Sir Edward Mutesa II**, as the first President in 1963.

blocks.x: Burundi and Rwanda

items: Both were ruled by **Belgium** after the First World War.
Both became independent on **1 July 1962**.
Burundi began as a kingdom and became a republic in 1966; Rwanda became a republic at independence.
Both suffered serious ethnic conflict afterwards, the worst being the **1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda**.

blocks.x: Why the Africans wanted independence

To **rule themselves** · to regain their **land** · to stop **forced labour and heavy taxes** · to end **racial discrimination** · to control their own **resources** · to restore **African dignity and culture** · to get better services, jobs and pay.
Methods used in the struggle

Forming **political parties** and **trade unions** · **strikes and boycotts** · **petitions and delegations** to the colonial government and to Britain · use of **newspapers** and public rallies · **armed struggle** where peaceful means failed, as in the Mau Mau · taking part in **elections** when they were allowed.
The first leaders of the independent countries

head: Country
First leader at independence
rows: **Milton Obote** (Prime Minister); Sir Edward Mutesa II, first President

blocks.x: Formation of republics
**Republic:** A country in which the head of state is a president chosen by the people, not a king.
Tanganyika became a republic in **1962**, Uganda in **1963** (and again under the 1967 constitution), Kenya in **1964**, Burundi in **1966**, and Rwanda at independence in **1962**.
Political parties today

Parties change with time, so learn the idea rather than only the names. Tanzania's ruling party has been **CCM (Chama Cha Mapinduzi)** since 1977; Uganda's is the **NRM**; Rwanda's is the **RPF**; Burundi's is the **CNDD–FDD**; Kenya has many parties that form coalitions at each election. All five countries today allow **multiparty politics**.
Challenges of post-independence East Africa

**Military coups** and unstable governments · **dictatorship** and abuse of human rights · **civil wars and rebellions** · the **1994 genocide against the Tutsi** in Rwanda · **tribalism and nepotism** · **corruption** · **poverty, unemployment and illiteracy** · **refugees** · heavy **foreign debts** · dependence on the export of raw materials · the collapse of the old EAC in 1977.

sections.title: 4. DEMOCRATIC RULE IN EAST AFRICAN COUNTRIES

blocks.x: Definitions
**Democracy:** Government of the people, by the people and for the people — a system in which people choose their leaders and take part in how they are governed.
**Citizen:** A full member of a country who owes it loyalty and enjoys its rights and protection.
The democratic process

Free and fair **elections** held regularly · **freedom of speech, assembly and the press** · respect for **human rights** and the **rule of law** · separation of powers between the **executive, legislature and judiciary** · accountability of leaders · involving people in decisions at village, district and national level.
Political and civic education

**Civic education** teaches citizens about their country, their constitution, their leaders, their rights and their duties, so that they can take part wisely. It is done through schools, radio, seminars, posters, drama and the Electoral Commission.
How one becomes a citizen
By **birth** · by **descent** (having a parent who is a citizen) · by **registration** (for example through marriage or long residence) · by **naturalisation**.
Rights and responsibilities of citizens

head: Basic rights
Responsibilities
rows: Obeying the laws of the country
Protecting public property and the environment
Defending the country and keeping peace
The right to **vote and to be voted for**
Reporting crime and being a good neighbour
Working hard and caring for one's family

blocks.x: The electoral process

items: **Voter registration** and display of the voters' register.
**Nomination** of candidates by the Electoral Commission.
**Campaigning** within the given period and rules.
**Polling day** — voters queue, are checked against the register, are marked with ink, and cast a **secret ballot**.
**Counting** the votes at the polling station in the presence of agents and observers.
**Declaring the results** by the returning officer and the Electoral Commission.
**Swearing in** of the winner; complaints go to the courts.

blocks.x: Challenges of the electoral process

**Rigging** and stuffing of ballot boxes · **bribery** of voters · **violence and intimidation** · **illiteracy**, so some voters cannot read the ballot · late delivery of materials and late opening of polling stations · **low voter turnout** · mistakes in the voters' register · shortage of **funds** · misuse of state resources · buying of voters' cards.
Solutions

Use a **strong, independent Electoral Commission** · use a **clean register** and modern identification · provide **civic and voter education** · deploy **observers, agents and police** · punish rigging and bribery · deliver materials on time · count and announce results openly · settle disputes through the **courts** rather than violence.

topics.title: Responsible Living in the East African Environment
topics.heading: TOPIC 5: RESPONSIBLE LIVING IN THE EAST AFRICAN ENVIRONMENT

blocks.x: *Curriculum reference: NCDC Primary Six Curriculum, Set One, Social Studies Topic 5, 15 periods (`curriculum/P6-SET-ONE-2010.pdf`, topic outline page 315 and pages 344–346).*

**What you already know:** In Topic 2 you saw how rich East Africa is in land, water, minerals and wildlife. In this last topic you learn how to **use those resources without destroying them**, and what happens when people live carelessly in the environment.
**By the end of this topic you should be able to:**

items: explain the sustainable use and conservation of the environment
describe proper methods of farming and the use of alternative energy
explain waste management, including recycling and sewage disposal
state the work of the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA)
explain climate change and the consequences of irresponsible living
suggest solutions to environmental problems in East Africa

blocks.x: Definitions
**Environment:** Everything that surrounds us — land, water, air, plants, animals and people.
**Environmental protection:** Taking care of the environment so that it is not damaged.
**Sustainable use:** Using resources carefully today in a way that leaves enough for the people of tomorrow.
**Conservation:** Protecting and looking after natural resources so that they are not used up or destroyed.
Sustainable use of the environment
**(a) Afforestation and reafforestation**

items: **Afforestation** — planting trees in an area where there were no trees before.
**Reafforestation** — replanting trees in an area where trees were cut down.
**Agroforestry** — growing trees together with crops and animals on the same land.

blocks.x: **(b) Proper methods of farming**

head: Method
What it does
rows: Changing the crop grown on a plot each season so the soil is not exhausted
Covering the soil with dry grass or leaves to hold moisture and stop erosion
Cutting steps on a hillside to slow running water
Ploughing across the slope instead of up and down
Planting crops in strips along the contour
Returning fertility to the soil naturally
Resting the land for a season to recover
Protecting the soil surface from rain and sun

blocks.x: **(c) Alternative energy use**

Instead of cutting trees for firewood and charcoal, people can use **solar energy, biogas, hydro-electric power, wind energy, energy-saving stoves and briquettes** made from waste. These save trees, produce less smoke and are cheaper in the long run.
**(d) Other conservation measures**

Gazetting **forest reserves, national parks and wetlands** · protecting **water catchment areas** · fighting **poaching** · controlling **bush burning** · educating the community · making and enforcing **environmental laws** · planting trees on public land and at school.
Definition
**Waste management:** The collecting, sorting, treating and disposing of rubbish and other waste in a safe way.
Types of waste

head: Type
Examples
rows: Food remains, peelings, leaves, paper, animal dung
Polythene bags (buveera), plastic bottles, glass, metal, batteries
Sewage, waste water from homes and factories
Chemicals, oils, used syringes and drugs

blocks.x: The good ways of handling waste

items: **Reduce** — buy and use less of what becomes rubbish, especially polythene.
**Reuse** — use containers, bottles, sacks and jerrycans again.
**Recycle** — turn waste into new things: plastic into basins, paper into new paper, metal into tools, old tyres into sandals.
**Composting** — rot food waste and peelings into manure for the garden.
**Sorting** — separate waste that rots from waste that does not.
**Sanitary landfills** — bury waste in a prepared pit far from homes and water.
**Incineration** — burn medical and dangerous waste in a proper incinerator.
**Sewage treatment** — treat sewage in ponds or plants before it reaches rivers and lakes.
**Using latrines and toilets** properly.
**Community clean-up days** and public rubbish skips.

blocks.x: Dangers of poor waste disposal

Blocked drainage and **flooding** · **diseases** such as cholera, typhoid, dysentery and malaria · **pollution** of soil, water and air · bad smells · injuries from broken glass and metal · death of animals and fish that swallow polythene · ugly surroundings that drive away tourists.
What it is

**NEMA** is the Ugandan government body responsible for the management of the environment. It was set up under the National Environment Act and started work in **1995**, with its offices in Kampala. Other East African countries have similar bodies — Kenya has **NEMA** too, and Tanzania has **NEMC**.
Functions of NEMA

items: **Coordinating and supervising** all environmental activities in the country.
Making and enforcing **environmental standards and regulations**.
Carrying out **environmental impact assessments** before big projects such as factories, dams and roads are built.
**Monitoring** pollution of air, water and land.
Protecting **wetlands, forests, river banks and lake shores**.
**Educating the public** about the environment.
**Advising government** on environmental policy.
**Punishing offenders** who break environmental laws.

blocks.x: Definition
**Climate change:** A long-term change in the normal climate of an area, such as rain becoming less reliable and temperatures rising.
Causes
**Deforestation** · **bush burning** · **swamp reclamation** · smoke from **factories and vehicles** · **overgrazing** · mining and quarrying · burning of fossil fuels · poor disposal of waste.
Signs and effects in East Africa

items: Rains that come **late, stop early or fail** altogether.
**Longer droughts**, especially in Karamoja and northern Kenya.
**Heavier storms and floods**, as in Kasese, Bududa and Kampala.
**Melting of the ice** on Mt Kilimanjaro and Rwenzori.
Lakes and rivers **drying up**; falling water levels affect hydro-electric power.
**Famine** and loss of pasture; conflicts over water and grazing land.
More **crop pests and diseases**.

sections.title: 5. CONSEQUENCES OF IRRESPONSIBLE LIVING IN THE EAST AFRICAN ENVIRONMENT

head: Consequence
How it happens
rows: Wetlands are filled in and drainage channels are blocked with rubbish
Farming on steep slopes after clearing the trees, as at Bududa
Overgrazing, tree cutting and bush burning turn land into semi-desert, as in parts of Karamoja
Factory waste, sewage, polythene, chemicals and smoke
Cholera and typhoid from dirty water; malaria from stagnant water; coughs from smoke and dust
Over-fishing, over-mining and over-cutting of forests leave nothing for the future
A very fast-growing population puts great pressure on land, forests, water and services
Bare soil is washed away by rain
Soil washed from gardens fills up the water bodies

items: **Afforestation and reafforestation**; every school and home planting trees.
Using **energy-saving stoves, biogas and solar** instead of firewood and charcoal.
**Proper farming methods** — terracing, mulching, crop rotation, contour ploughing.
**Protecting wetlands, river banks and lake shores** and stopping building in them.
**Proper waste management** — reduce, reuse, recycle, compost, and use sanitary landfills.
**Treating sewage and factory waste** before releasing it.
**Enforcing environmental laws** through NEMA, local councils and the police.
**Environmental education** in schools, on radio and in the community.
**Family planning education** to slow very rapid population growth.
**Resettling people** from dangerous slopes and flood-prone areas.
**Controlled grazing** and better livestock management.
Joint action across East Africa through the **EAC**, since air, lakes and rivers are shared.

blocks.x: What a P.6 learner can do

Plant and water a tree · use both sides of paper · pick up and sort rubbish · never burn polythene in the compound · use a latrine · switch off lights and use water sparingly · join the **school environment club** · tell others what you have learnt.

Meaning

items: **Afforestation** = new trees where there were none; **reafforestation** = replanting where trees were cut.
The three Rs of waste: **Reduce, Reuse, Recycle**.
**Polythene (buveera)** does not rot — it blocks drainage, kills animals and spoils soil.

Planting trees where there were none — afforestation.
The body that manages the environment in Uganda — NEMA.
One duty of NEMA — enforcing environmental laws (or carrying out impact assessments).
One method of soil conservation on a hill — terracing (or contour ploughing).

blocks.x: **Practice activity:** Draw a map of your school or village. Mark the rubbish pit, the latrines, the water source and the trees. Then write three things your class could do to improve the environment there.

items: Define the environment and environmental conservation.
Give the difference between afforestation and reafforestation.
Name any five proper methods of farming that protect the soil.
Give any four alternative sources of energy that save trees.
What is waste management?
Give the difference between biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste, with two examples of each.
Explain the three Rs of waste management.
Give any four dangers of poor waste disposal.
What does NEMA stand for, and in which year did it start work?
State any five functions of NEMA.
Define climate change and give any four of its causes.
Give any four effects of climate change in East Africa.
Give any five consequences of irresponsible living in the environment.
Why is it dangerous to build houses in a wetland?
Give any two causes of landslides and two ways of preventing them.
What is desertification, and which parts of East Africa are most affected?
Give any six solutions to the environmental problems of East Africa.
Give any four things a P.6 learner can do to protect the environment.
Why should the East African countries work together on environmental issues?
Draw a poster message of not more than ten words encouraging people to protect the environment.

The environment is everything that surrounds us — land, water, air, plants, animals and people. Conservation is protecting and looking after natural resources so that they are not used up or destroyed.
**Afforestation** is planting trees where there were none before, while **reafforestation** is replanting trees in an area where trees were cut down.
Any five of: crop rotation, mulching, terracing, contour ploughing, strip cropping, applying manure, controlled grazing, fallowing, planting cover crops.
Any four of: solar energy, biogas, hydro-electric power, wind energy, energy-saving stoves, briquettes.
Waste management is the collecting, sorting, treating and disposing of rubbish and other waste in a safe way.
**Biodegradable** waste rots naturally, for example food remains and leaves. **Non-biodegradable** waste does not rot, for example polythene bags and glass.
**Reduce** — use less of what becomes rubbish; **Reuse** — use items such as bottles and sacks again; **Recycle** — make waste into new useful things such as plastic basins from old plastic.

Any four of: blocked drainage and flooding; diseases such as cholera and malaria; pollution of soil, water and air; bad smells; injuries from broken glass; death of animals that swallow polythene; ugly surroundings.
**National Environment Management Authority**; it started work in **1995**.

Any five of: coordinating environmental activities; making and enforcing standards; carrying out environmental impact assessments; monitoring pollution; protecting wetlands and forests; educating the public; advising government; punishing offenders.
Climate change is a long-term change in the normal climate of an area. Causes: deforestation, bush burning, swamp reclamation, smoke from factories and vehicles, overgrazing (any four).
Any four of: unreliable rainfall; longer droughts; heavier storms and floods; melting of ice on Kilimanjaro and Rwenzori; drying lakes and rivers; famine; more crop pests.

Any five of: floods, landslides, desertification, pollution of land, water and air, diseases, resource depletion, pressure from a very fast-growing population, loss of wildlife, soil erosion, silting of lakes.

Because a wetland holds water like a sponge. When it is filled in and built on, the water has nowhere to go, so the area **floods**; the houses stand on weak, waterlogged ground; the wetland can no longer filter water or provide fish, papyrus and water for the community.

**Causes:** cutting trees and farming on steep slopes; heavy prolonged rain on loose soil (also digging and building on steep ground). **Prevention:** plant trees and grass on steep slopes; make terraces and dig contour trenches; avoid cultivating and settling on very steep land; resettle people from dangerous slopes.
Desertification is the spread of desert conditions into land that was not desert before. It affects **Karamoja in Uganda and northern Kenya** most (also parts of central Tanzania).

Any six of: afforestation and reafforestation; energy-saving stoves, biogas and solar; proper farming methods; protecting wetlands and river banks; proper waste management; treating sewage and factory waste; enforcing laws through NEMA; environmental education; family planning education; resettling people from dangerous areas; joint EAC action.

Any four of: plant and water a tree; use both sides of paper; pick up and sort rubbish; never burn polythene; use a latrine; save water and switch off lights; join the school environment club; teach others.

Because the environment is **shared** — Lake Victoria, the River Nile, the air and the migrating wildlife cross borders. Pollution or deforestation in one country affects the others, so laws, research and clean-up efforts work best when the countries act together through the EAC.
*Learner's poster.* For example: **"Plant a tree today, save your tomorrow."**
**Afforestation** (new trees) vs **reafforestation** (replanting)
Farming care: crop rotation · mulching · terracing · contour ploughing · manure
Energy that saves trees: **solar · biogas · energy-saving stoves**
Waste: **Reduce · Reuse · Recycle** · compost · sanitary landfill · treat sewage
**NEMA** — Uganda's environment authority, started **1995**, does impact assessments
Climate change: deforestation, bush burning, swamp draining, smoke
Careless living → floods · landslides (Bududa) · desertification (Karamoja) · pollution · disease
